title: Newmarket shooting suicide by cop, chief says
article: An inquest jury has recommended York Regional Police and the province take a closer look at whether suspects should be contacted before being arrested.
But York's police chief said every situation is different.

The three-man, two-woman jury made its recommendation after deliberating Wednesday in the death of Evan Arnold, 26, of Newmarket, who was shot dead by York police in 2006. The three-day inquest was held at Aurora's Town Hall.
The jury recommended policies and procedures in order to determine if calling a suspect before an arrest is appropriate.
York police currently do not have a specific policy about calling people before an arrest is made and are unlikely to create one, Chief Armand La Barge said.
However, the Newmarket shooting will provide invaluable real-life experience that instructors can pass on in training, the chief added.
He also expects his officers will think about Mr. Arnold's death when contemplating calling a suspect and make a decision on a case-by-case basis, he said.
Meanwhile, Mr. Arnold's mother Anne Arnold, an East Gwillimbury resident, told The Era she was happy with the outcome.
"I think it's important that (police) know everything. "So, perhaps they could do it in a better way," she said.

Arrests often occur at homes, workplaces, crime scenes and in other public areas, the chief said. Arrests at homes can traumatize families, while arrests at workplaces can offend some people, he added. A phone call before the arrest could cause someone to surrender or meet police somewhere else.
"Sometimes, all you have is a cellphone number."
However, if a suspect is considered a flight risk, an officer likely wouldn't try to reach that person by telephone.
"You have to examine each case, each individual suspect," he said.
Along with the recommendation to York police and the province, the inquest jury had to answer several questions, including by what means Mr. Arnold died.
The jury ruled his death a homicide - a ruling the chief disagreed with.
"In my mind, this was the clearest case of suicide by cop I have ever seen," he said. "I commend the officers for using the patience they did. He wanted us to shoot him."
The inquest had heard a York officer contacted Mr. Arnold to let him know she planned to arrest him for sexual assault.
Mr. Arnold told the officer he was in Newmarket and walking home.
He told the officer her call was a "long time coming" and that he was going to "end it all", the inquest heard.
Const. Morgan didn't know exactly where Mr. Arnold was when they spoke and testified she considered calling for York tactical officers.
She had no idea before speaking with Mr. Arnold that afternoon that he was suicidal, she testified.
The circumstances surrounding the sexual assault investigation were not discussed during the inquest.
Later that day, Mr. Arnold broke into a Southwind Court home.
Mr. Arnold told the homeowner the police were after him and ordered her out of her home.

Officers responded and with guns drawn, surrounded the house. One officer ran up the driveway and tried to open the front door but it was locked. He was about to walk away when the man, holding two large knives, opened the door.
Police yelled at him to drop the knives but he told them if they didn't kill him, he would kill an officer.
Mr. Arnold lunged at an officer, who shot twice, striking Mr. Arnold in the chest.
He later died at Southlake Regional Health Centre.
The officer who shot and killed Mr. Arnold had no other choice but to fire, the inquest heard.
On Thursday, the province had not received the inquest jury recommendation, Stuart McGetrick, spokesperson for the Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services said.
"When we do formally receive them, we will be carefully reviewing them before responding," he said.
Mr. McGetrick added the province has no time line as to when it plans to respond to the Arnold inquest recommendation.
